title: Lactulose for Hepatic Encephalopathy: Titrate to Mental-Status Protection
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Lactulose is a poorly absorbed disaccharide used as a colonic acidifier to reduce ammonia burden in portal-systemic encephalopathy. The nursing goal is clinical improvement without causing severe diarrhea, dehydration, or electrolyte disturbance.
recognize: Improved orientation and less asterixis suggest response; excessive watery stool can create dehydration and hypokalemia.
Worsening confusion despite therapy requires evaluation for triggers such as infection, GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration, or sedatives.
priorities: Track mental status and stool response rather than treating the medication as a simple laxative.
Escalate worsening encephalopathy, aspiration risk, or severe volume/electrolyte loss.
assessMonitor: Monitor cognition, stool pattern, hydration, sodium/potassium, abdominal distention, and precipitating causes.
interventions: Administer by the prescribed route and support hydration/electrolyte replacement as ordered.
medicationSafety: Excessive dosing can cause diarrhea, dehydration, hypernatremia, or hypokalemia.
Do not delay evaluation of deteriorating mental status just to give more lactulose.
teaching: The goal in encephalopathy is improved thinking with the prescribed bowel-response target, not uncontrolled diarrhea.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and trend stool/mental status; acute neurologic deterioration requires RN/provider escalation.
examTrap: Treating escalating confusion by endlessly increasing laxative exposure without evaluating the cause.
oneLinePearl: Lactulose protects the brain by changing the gut—too much can destabilize the patient.
sourceBasis: DailyMed lactulose solution labeling updated 2026-01 to 2026-05

title: Rifaximin: Gut-Directed Antibiotic for Recurrent Hepatic Encephalopathy
bottomLine: Rifaximin is a minimally absorbed gut-directed antibiotic used to reduce recurrence of overt hepatic encephalopathy in appropriate adults. It complements, rather than replaces, assessment for active precipitants of encephalopathy.
recognize: Persistent or new confusion despite rifaximin still requires evaluation for infection, bleeding, constipation, dehydration, sedatives, and metabolic problems.
Systemic drug exposure can increase with severe hepatic impairment.
priorities: Verify indication and concurrent hepatic-encephalopathy plan.
Escalate new mental-status deterioration rather than assuming the maintenance drug has failed by itself.
assessMonitor: Monitor cognition, recurrence pattern, adherence, hepatic status, and significant drug interactions.
interventions: Administer consistently and reinforce the broader prevention plan.
medicationSafety: Not a substitute for urgent evaluation of acute encephalopathy.
Use caution with severe hepatic impairment and relevant interacting drugs.
teaching: Continue prescribed bowel and liver-management measures; report recurrent confusion promptly.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and observe trends; changing consciousness requires escalation.
examTrap: Assuming rifaximin means other causes of acute confusion no longer need investigation.
oneLinePearl: Rifaximin prevents recurrence; it does not explain every episode of confusion.

title: Ursodiol: Bile-Acid Therapy for Primary Biliary Cholangitis
bottomLine: Ursodiol is bile-acid therapy used for primary biliary cholangitis and selected gallstone indications. It is long-term disease-modifying therapy, not an acute treatment for biliary obstruction or cholangitis.
recognize: Persistent jaundice, fever, or RUQ pain can signal complications that ursodiol will not rapidly correct.
Bile-acid sequestrants can reduce ursodiol absorption if taken too close together.
priorities: Verify indication and assess liver-disease trajectory.
Escalate acute obstruction/infection symptoms rather than waiting for chronic therapy to work.
assessMonitor: Trend liver tests and clinical symptoms as ordered; review interacting bile-acid sequestrants and adherence.
interventions: Administer with food when prescribed and separate from interacting sequestrants according to product/provider instructions.
medicationSafety: Chronic therapy requires monitoring; it does not dissolve every gallstone or resolve acute obstruction.
Review aluminum-containing antacids and bile-acid sequestrant timing.
teaching: Take consistently and keep laboratory follow-up; report fever, severe abdominal pain, or worsening jaundice.
delegationScope: PNs may reinforce adherence and monitor symptoms; decompensation or suspected cholangitis requires escalation.
examTrap: Using ursodiol as the emergency treatment for an acutely obstructed infected biliary tree.
oneLinePearl: Ursodiol is chronic bile therapy, not acute source control.

title: Cholestyramine: Bile-Acid Binding and Medication-Separation Safety
bottomLine: Cholestyramine binds bile acids in the gut and can be used for selected lipid or bile-acid-related symptoms. Its biggest nursing safety issue is that it can bind other medications and impair absorption.
recognize: Constipation, bloating, and poor palatability can reduce adherence.
Warfarin, thyroid hormone, digoxin, and many other drugs can have altered absorption when taken too close to cholestyramine.
priorities: Review the full medication schedule before administration.
Assess constipation risk and bowel obstruction history.
assessMonitor: Monitor bowel pattern, adherence, lipid or symptom response, and effects of interacting medications.
interventions: Mix powder exactly as directed; do not give dry powder and separate interacting oral medicines according to prescribing guidance.
medicationSafety: Can reduce absorption of many drugs and fat-soluble vitamins.
Use caution in severe constipation or obstruction risk.
redFlags: Severe abdominal distention or no stool/flatus
teaching: Keep other medicines on the timing schedule provided by the pharmacist/prescriber.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and reinforce spacing; clinically important interaction effects require provider/pharmacist review.
examTrap: Administering all morning medications mixed together with cholestyramine.
oneLinePearl: Cholestyramine binds bile—and can bind the patient’s other medicines too.

title: Linaclotide: Secretagogue Therapy and Diarrhea Risk
bottomLine: Linaclotide is a guanylate-cyclase-C agonist used for selected constipation syndromes. Severe diarrhea and age restrictions are the major medication-safety issues.
recognize: Diarrhea is the most common adverse effect and can cause dehydration.
Mechanical GI obstruction is a contraindication.
priorities: Screen for obstruction symptoms before giving and monitor stool response/hydration.
Escalate severe diarrhea, syncope, or dehydration.
assessMonitor: Monitor bowel pattern, abdominal pain/distention, hydration, and electrolyte concerns if diarrhea is significant.
interventions: Administer according to product timing instructions and hold/escalate severe diarrhea per prescribed plan.
medicationSafety: Contraindicated in known/suspected mechanical GI obstruction.
Do not use outside approved pediatric age restrictions.
teaching: Report severe diarrhea and maintain hydration as instructed.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and trend bowel response; suspected obstruction or severe dehydration requires escalation.
examTrap: Giving a secretagogue to a patient with suspected mechanical bowel obstruction.
oneLinePearl: Before treating constipation, rule out obstruction.

title: Lubiprostone: Chloride-Channel Activation and Nausea/Hypotension Safety
bottomLine: Lubiprostone activates intestinal chloride channels to increase fluid secretion in selected constipation disorders. Nausea, diarrhea, dyspnea after dosing, and syncope/hypotension are important nursing safety cues.
recognize: Nausea is common and may improve when taken with food and water.
Transient dyspnea, chest tightness, hypotension, or syncope can occur after dosing.
priorities: Exclude mechanical obstruction and assess baseline volume status.
Escalate syncope, severe dyspnea, or persistent severe diarrhea.
assessMonitor: Monitor stool pattern, nausea, hydration, blood-pressure symptoms, and breathing symptoms after doses.
interventions: Administer with food/water as directed and swallow capsules intact.
medicationSafety: Contraindicated in known/suspected mechanical obstruction.
Monitor for severe diarrhea and hypotension.
teaching: Take with food/water if directed and report fainting or severe breathing difficulty.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; acute cardiopulmonary symptoms require escalation.
examTrap: Treating post-dose dyspnea as an expected symptom that never needs assessment.
oneLinePearl: Lubiprostone treats constipation, but syncope or dyspnea are not routine bowel effects.

title: Dicyclomine: Antispasmodic Benefit and Anticholinergic Burden
bottomLine: Dicyclomine is an anticholinergic antispasmodic used for functional bowel spasm. The nursing priority is recognizing anticholinergic toxicity and avoiding use in patients where reduced gut/urinary/ocular motility is dangerous.
recognize: Dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, confusion, and heat intolerance reflect anticholinergic effects.
Older adults are especially vulnerable to confusion, falls, and urinary retention.
priorities: Review glaucoma, urinary retention/BPH, bowel obstruction/ileus, myasthenia gravis, and anticholinergic medication burden.
Escalate acute confusion, urinary retention, or ileus symptoms.
assessMonitor: Monitor bowel sounds/pattern, urinary output, cognition, vision complaints, heart rate, and heat exposure risk.
interventions: Administer only for the intended functional-spasm indication and avoid masking acute abdominal emergencies.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergic burden increases fall/delirium/retention risk.
Not appropriate for suspected obstructive or inflammatory emergencies.
teaching: Avoid overheating and report urinary difficulty, severe constipation, or vision changes.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; acute abdominal or neurologic changes require escalation.
examTrap: Giving dicyclomine to quiet severe abdominal pain before ruling out obstruction or peritonitis.
oneLinePearl: Antispasmodic does not mean safe in an obstructed gut.

title: Oral Budesonide for IBD: Local Steroid Intent, Systemic Steroid Risks
bottomLine: Oral delayed/extended-release budesonide formulations deliver corticosteroid activity to selected intestinal regions for IBD. Despite high first-pass metabolism, systemic steroid adverse effects and adrenal suppression remain possible.
recognize: Infection, hyperglycemia, mood change, bruising, hypertension, and adrenal suppression can still occur.
Formulations are not interchangeable because release location matters.
priorities: Verify the exact product/formulation and indication.
Review infection risk and other corticosteroid exposure.
assessMonitor: Monitor bowel symptoms, infection, glucose/BP when relevant, steroid adverse effects, and adrenal-insufficiency cues during taper/transition.
interventions: Administer the exact prescribed formulation without crushing products that require intact release characteristics.
medicationSafety: Do not assume 'gut-selective' means free of systemic corticosteroid risk.
Avoid abrupt discontinuation after significant prolonged exposure unless the prescriber directs it.
teaching: Use the exact product prescribed and do not stop long-term steroid therapy abruptly without guidance.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; steroid taper decisions remain prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Treating oral budesonide as though it has no systemic steroid effects.
oneLinePearl: Budesonide is more local—not purely local.
sourceBasis: Current FDA-approved oral budesonide IBD labeling

title: Vedolizumab: Gut-Selective Biologic With Infection and PML Vigilance
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Vedolizumab is an integrin-receptor antagonist used for ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease. Safe nursing care requires infection screening, hypersensitivity/infusion monitoring, liver-injury recognition, and vigilance for new neurologic symptoms despite its gut-selective mechanism.
recognize: Serious infection can occur and active severe infection may require holding therapy per prescriber guidance.
New progressive neurologic deficits require urgent evaluation for rare PML concern.
priorities: Assess for active infection before administration and verify vaccination/specialty plan.
Escalate severe infusion reaction, jaundice, or new neurologic change.
assessMonitor: Monitor infection symptoms, infusion/injection reactions, liver symptoms/labs when ordered, and neurologic status.
interventions: Administer IV or SC formulation per product and facility protocol when authorized.
medicationSafety: Do not give through serious uncontrolled infection without specialty guidance.
Do not dismiss progressive neurologic symptoms because the drug is gut selective.
redFlags: New progressive weakness, vision, speech, or cognitive change
teaching: Report infection symptoms and any new neurologic changes promptly.
delegationScope: Biologic administration authority varies by state/facility; PN role centers monitoring, safe implementation, and escalation.
examTrap: Assuming a gut-selective biologic eliminates systemic infection or neurologic safety concerns.
oneLinePearl: Gut selective is not risk free.

title: Prucalopride: Prokinetic Constipation Therapy and Psychiatric Safety
bottomLine: Prucalopride is a selective serotonin-4 receptor agonist used for chronic idiopathic constipation. The key nursing safety points are obstruction exclusion, renal-dose awareness, and monitoring for new or worsening depression or suicidal thoughts.
recognize: Headache, abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea are common early effects.
Mood or behavioral changes require prompt assessment.
priorities: Exclude mechanical obstruction and review renal function.
Escalate suicidal ideation or severe psychiatric change immediately.
assessMonitor: Monitor bowel response, hydration, renal function context, mood, and suicidal thinking.
interventions: Administer consistently and coordinate prescriber review if significant diarrhea or psychiatric symptoms emerge.
medicationSafety: Contraindicated in intestinal perforation/obstruction or severe inflammatory obstructive conditions per labeling.
Dose adjustment may be needed in severe renal impairment.
complications: Treatment failure if obstruction is missed
teaching: Report new depression, unusual mood changes, or suicidal thoughts promptly.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; suicidality or obstruction signs require urgent escalation.
examTrap: Treating a patient’s severe obstructive symptoms with a stronger prokinetic before evaluating the obstruction.
oneLinePearl: Before stimulating motility, make sure the bowel is open—and monitor the mind too.
